title: Risk: CFS shuns Australian private credit market
full_text:
The Australian private credit sector is so concentrated with risky property development assets that one of the nation's largest superannuation funds, the $180 billion Colonial First State, will only invest overseas.
The candid assessment comes as the broader pension sector distances itself from the opaque and illiquid asset class after the $3.4 billion collapse of Western Sydney property developer Bathla exposed several top private credit firms and underlined the broader sector's vulnerability to sinking real estate values.
CFS chief investment officer Jonathan Armitage said that he only backed private credit managers in the United States and Europe, given they loaned to more stable companies in a wider array of industries with less competition.
"We saw more concentration risk in single names, but critically you did see concentration risks by sectors," Armitage said, referring to his avoidance of Australian private credit managers.
"In the United States, somewhere between 6 per cent and 10 per cent of all private credit is real estate-related. Here in Australia, it is 50 per cent," he said, while acknowledging that the figure somewhat depends on what is defined as private credit.
Private credit acts as a shadow banking market, extending high-interest loans to businesses that otherwise cannot secure lending from traditional banks. The lenders raise money for the loans from institutional and retail investors.
It was the main source of funding for Bathla, which failed owing $3.4 billion to creditors and leaving 2500 half-built apartments and a pipeline of another 14,000 homes in limbo.
ASIC commissioner Simone Constant said earlier this week that Bathla signals "significant cracks - the first stress fractures - beginning to emerge" in the domestic private credit market.
Constant warned that the sector had "tried to run before it could walk" and had ignored her repeated warnings to more fairly value the assets it was invested in, rather than inflating them to maintain high management fees.
She urged superannuation trustees and institutional investors not to "treat private credit as an easy, high-yielding substitute for traditional fixed-income investments while accepting manager marks at face value". "Trustees must look past headline returns, examine the underlying collateral, verify bad-debt provisioning and independently test manager assumptions before committing member capital."
Reserve Bank of Australia governor Michele Bullock last week told a parliamentary committee she had growing concerns about the global links between private credit and the mainstream financial system, and the potential contagion risks.
Although, RBA assistant governor Brad Jones, told the same committee that private credit did not pose a systemic threat to the Australian banking system or economy.
The Australian Financial Review asked 10 of the largest superannuation funds, which manage more than $1.5 trillion in assets, if they had any exposure to Bathla. They all said that no member money was at risk.
Australian Retirement Trust, the country's second-biggest fund, confirmed to Bloomberg it had $14 million exposed to the collapse via its investment in Bathla lender PAG.
Armitage said that private credit had become incredibly popular in Australia as interest rates trended down to record lows in 2022, pushing investors to chase the higher-yielding assets as opposed to government bonds without understanding the underlying risk.
"Some investors may have bought into these assets not understanding the illiquidity that comes with it. These are not traded instruments. You are not buying a piece of corporate debt that can be traded," he said. "In the desire to find some more attractive yields, that illiquidity may have been forgotten by some participants."
